## Association Between Injection and Microseismicity in Geothermal Fields With Multiple Wells: Data‐Driven Modeling of Rotokawa, New Zealand, and Húsmúli, Iceland

Yu, Pengliang, Dempsey, David, Rinaldi, Antonio Pio, Calibugan, Aimee, Ritz, Vanille A., Archer, Rosalind (2023). Association Between Injection and Microseismicity in Geothermal Fields With Multiple Wells: Data‐Driven Modeling of Rotokawa, New Zealand, and Húsmúli, Iceland. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 128(4), e2022JB025952. https://doi.org/10.1029/2022jb025952
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-yu-association-injection-microseismicity-geothermal-fields/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-yu-association-injection-microseismicity-geothermal-fields/yu2023-association-injection-microseismicity.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-yu-association-injection-microseismicity-geothermal-fields/fulltext.md
We used data-driven methods to find which injection wells are associated with small earthquakes at the Rotokawa (New Zealand) and Húsmúli (Iceland) fields. Injection was more closely associated with earthquake rates averaged over weeks than over days. At Rotokawa, we found no evidence that rapid injection changes trigger earthquakes.

- At Rotokawa, both methods associated injection into Well
- At Húsmúli, wells HN-17 and HN-12 and the carbon dioxide stream of well HN-16 were the injectors most associated with microseismicity, although these associations could be spurious.
- Injection was more strongly associated with earthquake rates averaged over weeks than over a few days. At Rotokawa, random variation is likely to dominate over a few days.
- Cumulative injected volume and injection rate appeared to be the most informative data. At Rotokawa, we found no evidence that rapid changes in injection rate trigger earthquakes.
- The machine learning method offered only marginal benefit over a simple regression model. Both identified broadly the same wells.

Abstract: Understanding injection‐induced microseismicity in geothermal systems can provide insight into reservoir connectedness. However, fault and reservoir complexity are difficult to represent in simple analytical models, which makes it difficult to discern clear relationships from incidental associations. Here, we have used data‐driven models to study how fluid injection and microseismicity are related in the Rotokawa (New Zealand) and Hellisheiði (Iceland) geothermal fields. We tested two classes of model: (a) lagged linear regression of seismicity rate as a function of well injection rates; and (b) systematic extraction of injection time series features that are then evaluated for associations with the seismicity. These models allowed us to determine which wells had the greatest correlation with microseismicity and to explain this association in a reservoir context. Finally, exploring different data types and transformations, we were unable to establish a link between rapid changes in injection rate and seismicity spikes, as suggested by some theoretical models.

## Identification of Seismo‐Volcanic Regimes at Whakaari/White Island (New Zealand) Via Systematic Tuning of an Unsupervised Classifier

Steinke, B., Jolly, A. D., Carniel, R., Dempsey, D. E., Cronin, S. J. (2023). Identification of Seismo‐Volcanic Regimes at Whakaari/White Island (New Zealand) Via Systematic Tuning of an Unsupervised Classifier. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 128(3), e2022JB026221. https://doi.org/10.1029/2022jb026221
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-steinke-identification-seismo-volcanic-regimes-whakaari/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-steinke-identification-seismo-volcanic-regimes-whakaari/steinke2023-identification-seismo-volcanic.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-steinke-identification-seismo-volcanic-regimes-whakaari/fulltext.md
We tuned an unsupervised classifier on 12.5 years of volcanic tremor at Whakaari. It separated background from unrest. In a retrospective analysis, its output changed to unrest regimes 6 weeks before the August 2012 eruption and about 3.5 months before the December 2019 eruption.

- Statistical tests on classifier settings guided our choice of five clusters, 12-hour windows, a 2 to 5 Hz frequency band and a map of 5 by 5 neurons.
- One cluster, usually with the lowest tremor levels, dominated the earliest and latest stages, and in our retrospective analysis ceased to dominate 6 weeks before the August 2012 eruption.
- The background cluster ceased to dominate about 3.5 months before the December 2019 eruption.
- We hypothesise that the unrest regimes represent pressurisation, depressurisation, and surface activity with free degassing, in a similar order in 2012/2013 and 2019.
- We propose that the different regime pattern before the 2016 eruption resulted from rapid destabilisation of the shallow hydrothermal system.

Abstract: We present an algorithm based on Self‐Organizing Maps (SOM) and k‐means clustering to recognize patterns in a continuous 12.5‐year tremor time series recorded at Whakaari/White Island volcano, New Zealand (hereafter referred to as Whakaari). The approach is extendable to a variety of volcanic settings through systematic tuning of the classifier. Hyperparameters are evaluated by statistical means, yielding a combination of “ideal” SOM parameters for the given data set. Extending from this, we applied a Kernel Density Estimation approach to automatically detect changes within the observed seismicity. We categorize the Whakaari seismic time series into regimes representing distinct volcano‐seismic states during recent unrest episodes at Whakaari (2012/2013, 2016, and 2019). There is a clear separation in classification results between background regimes and those representing elevated levels of unrest. Onset of unrest is detected by the classifier 6 weeks before the August 2012 eruption, and ca. 3.5 months before the December 2019 eruption, respectively. Regime changes are corroborated by changes in commonly monitored tremor proxies as well as with reported volcanic activity. The regimes are hypothesized to represent diverse mechanisms including: system pressurization and depressurization, degassing, and elevated surface activity. Labeling these regimes improves visualization of the 2012/2013 and 2019 unrest and eruptive episodes. The pre‐eruptive 2016 unrest showed a contrasting shape and nature of seismic regimes, suggesting differing onset and driving processes. The 2016 episode is proposed to result from rapid destabilization of the shallow hydrothermal system, while rising magmatic gases from new injections of magma better explain the 2012/2013 and 2019 episodes.

## Physics-Based Forecasting of Induced Seismicity at Groningen Gas Field, The Netherlands: Post Hoc Evaluation and Forecast Update

Dempsey, David E., Suckale, Jenny (2023). Physics-Based Forecasting of Induced Seismicity at Groningen Gas Field, The Netherlands: Post Hoc Evaluation and Forecast Update. Seismological Research Letters. https://doi.org/10.1785/0220220317
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-dempsey-physics-forecasting-induced-seismicity-groningen/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-dempsey-physics-forecasting-induced-seismicity-groningen/dempsey2023-physics-forecasting-induced.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-dempsey-physics-forecasting-induced-seismicity-groningen/fulltext.md
We tested our 2017 earthquake forecast for the Groningen gas field against the earthquakes that followed, then updated it. For 2021 to 2030, the largest event has a 1% chance of exceeding magnitude 3.8 if ruptures are confined to the reservoir, and 5.4 if they can extend below it.

- Because gas extraction from February 2017 to July 2022 was about 35% less than the lowest scenario in our 2017 forecast, we scaled that forecast by the volume extracted.
- After scaling, the 2017 forecast slightly underestimated the number of earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or more, with the 10 observed at about its 2% exceedance level.
- The largest earthquake from February 2017 to July 2022, a magnitude 3.4, was consistent with the 2017 forecast.
- We calibrated the updated model on earthquakes before 2017 and found no clear evidence to reject it in tests against the 2017 to 2022 record.
- For 2021 to 2030, the largest earthquake has a 1% chance of exceeding magnitude 3.8 if ruptures are confined to the reservoir, the scenario we prefer, and 5.4 otherwise.

## Carbon negative geothermal: Theoretical efficiency and sequestration potential of geothermal-BECCS energy cycles

Titus, K.A., Dempsey, D.E., Peer, R.A.M. (2023). Carbon negative geothermal: Theoretical efficiency and sequestration potential of geothermal-BECCS energy cycles. International Journal of Greenhouse Gas Control, 122, 103813. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijggc.2022.103813
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-titus-carbon-negative-geothermal-theoretical-efficiency/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-titus-carbon-negative-geothermal-theoretical-efficiency/titus2023-carbon-negative-geothermal.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2023-titus-carbon-negative-geothermal-theoretical-efficiency/fulltext.md
We modelled four power plant designs that burn forestry waste alongside a 160 °C geothermal resource and dissolve the flue CO2 in reinjected water. Per kg/s of geofluid drawn, they generated 62–589 kWe, the top figure mostly from biomass, and could store 217–675 tonnes of CO2 a year.

- In our model, adding a biomass boiler increased output per kg/s of 160 °C geofluid from 32–43 kWe in conventional plants to 62–76 kWe.
- A biomass steam plant that uses geofluid to preheat its water generated 589 kWe per kg/s of geofluid and needed 19% less biomass than the same plant without geofluid.
- Water reinjected at 95 °C and 50 bar can dissolve 0.021 kg of CO2 per kg, enough for all the flue CO2 of three designs and 17% of the fourth.
- We estimate operational emissions intensities of −131 to −922 g of CO2 per kWh, where negative means more CO2 is stored than emitted.
- Scaled up, a 124 MWe plant of Configuration 3, which splits biomass-heated geofluid between a steam turbine and a binary unit, could sequester 1 Mt of CO2 a year.

## Active distributed temperature sensing to assess surface water–groundwater interaction and river loss in braided river systems

Banks, Eddie W., Morgan, Leanne K., Sai Louie, Alice J., Dempsey, David, Wilson, Scott R. (2022). Active distributed temperature sensing to assess surface water–groundwater interaction and river loss in braided river systems. Journal of Hydrology, 615, 128667. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2022.128667
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-banks-active-distributed-temperature-sensing-assess/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-banks-active-distributed-temperature-sensing-assess/banks2022-active-distributed-temperature.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-banks-active-distributed-temperature-sensing-assess/fulltext.md
We installed heated fibre optic cables 5 m beneath the Waikirikiri Selwyn River, a braided river in Canterbury, to measure water leaking from the river into the gravels below. We estimate that groundwater beneath the channel moved at an average of 12.0 and 15.8 m per day in two surveys.

- Two 100 m long drillholes, about 5 m below and across the river channel, contain fibre optic cables that we heated at 15 W per metre for 20 minutes.
- Fitting a heat transport solution to the warming at every 0.25 m of cable gave average groundwater velocities of 12.0 and 15.8 m per day in two surveys.
- If that flow is vertical, river water entered the shallow aquifer at about 2.8 cubic metres per square metre per day.
- Because velocities varied little across the 60 m wide channel, we suggest that buried former channels have only a small effect on groundwater flow paths at our site.
- For the first survey, 20% changes in most assumed inputs gave 9.6 to 14.4 m per day against 12.0, and a 12 s later heating start gave 15.4.

## Evaluation of short-term probabilistic eruption forecasting at Whakaari, New Zealand

Dempsey, D. E., Kempa-Liehr, A. W., Ardid, A., Li, A., Orenia, S., Singh, J., Tyler, A. J., Cronin, S. J. (2022). Evaluation of short-term probabilistic eruption forecasting at Whakaari, New Zealand. Bulletin of Volcanology, 84(10), 91. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00445-022-01600-5
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-dempsey-evaluation-short-term-probabilistic-eruption/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-dempsey-evaluation-short-term-probabilistic-eruption/dempsey2022-evaluation-short-term.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-dempsey-evaluation-short-term-probabilistic-eruption/fulltext.md
We ran an eruption forecaster at Whakaari for 18 months and filtered out the earthquakes that caused its three false positives. In a test with the 2019 eruption withheld from training, a calibrated version gave a 2 to 4% chance in 48 hours, up to 400 times its lowest level.

- Between February 2020 and August 2021 our real-time forecaster raised three false positives, all caused by regional earthquakes. No eruptions occurred.
- With earthquake filtering and data normalisation added, the improved model would have raised none of those three false positives.
- A warning system tested on eruptions withheld from training warned of six of seven eruptions, with warnings in effect about 14 days a year.
- During a warning the chance of eruption was 8.1% in 48 hours, 126 times higher than outside a warning.
- Over 2 to 18 December 2019, expert estimates of a second eruption scored worse than a fixed forecast based on the 2011 to 2019 average eruption rate.

Abstract: Phreatic explosions at volcanoes are difficult to forecast but can be locally devastating, as illustrated by the deadly 2019 Whakaari (New Zealand) eruption. Quantifying eruption likelihood is essential for risk calculations that underpin volcano access decisions and disaster response. But estimating eruption probabilities is notoriously difficult for sudden onset eruptions. Here, we describe two retrospectively developed models for short-term (48 h) probabilistic forecasting of phreatic eruptions at Whakaari. The models are based on a pseudo-prospective analysis of seven Whakaari eruptions whose precursors were identified by time series feature engineering of continuous seismic data. The first model, an optimized warning system, could anticipate six out of seven eruptions at the cost of 14 warning days each year. While a warning is in effect, the probability of eruption is about 8% in 48 h, which is about 126 times higher than outside the warning. The second model used isotonic calibration to translate the output of the forecast model onto a probability scale. When applied pseudo-prospectively in the 48 h prior to the December 2019 eruption, it indicated an eruption probability up to 400 times higher than the background. Finally, we quantified the accuracy of these seismic data-driven forecasts, alongside an observatory expert elicitation that used multiple data sources. To do this, we used a forecast skill score that was benchmarked against the average rate of eruptions at Whakaari between 2011 and 2019. This exercise highlights the conditions under which the three different forecasting approaches perform well and where potential improvements could be made.

## Seismic precursors to the Whakaari 2019 phreatic eruption are transferable to other eruptions and volcanoes

Ardid, Alberto, Dempsey, David, Caudron, Corentin, Cronin, Shane (2022). Seismic precursors to the Whakaari 2019 phreatic eruption are transferable to other eruptions and volcanoes. Nature Communications, 13(1), 2002. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29681-y
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-ardid-seismic-precursors-whakaari-2019-phreatic/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-ardid-seismic-precursors-whakaari-2019-phreatic/ardid2022-seismic-precursors-whakaari.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-ardid-seismic-precursors-whakaari-2019-phreatic/fulltext.md
We searched seismic tremor recorded before 18 eruptions at six volcanoes for a shared precursor. A rise in the ratio of medium- to high-frequency tremor recurred before steam-driven eruptions at Whakaari and, less clearly, Ruapehu and Tongariro. At Whakaari in 2019, we interpret it as shallow sealing and pressurisation.

- We analysed a combined 50 years of seismic tremor from six volcanoes in New Zealand, Alaska and Kamchatka, covering the weeks before 18 eruptions.
- The 48-hour median of the medium- to high-frequency tremor ratio rose to a peak about 2 to 4 days before eruptions at several volcanoes.
- Before each of four other Whakaari eruptions, this pattern resembled the 2019 pattern more closely than 90% of four-week periods without eruptions.
- The pattern was partly transferable to steam-driven eruptions at Ruapehu and Tongariro. For magmatic eruptions in Alaska and Kamchatka, results were not clearly different from a random benchmark.
- We interpret the 2019 Whakaari signal as a hydrothermal seal forming and shallow groundwater pressurising in the final week, with the seal failing over the last 16 hours.

Abstract: Volcanic eruptions that occur without warning can be deadly in touristic and populated areas. Even with real-time geophysical monitoring, forecasting sudden eruptions is difficult, because their precursors are hard to recognize and can vary between volcanoes. Here, we describe a general seismic precursor signal for gas-driven eruptions, identified through correlation analysis of 18 well-recorded eruptions in New Zealand, Alaska, and Kamchatka. The precursor manifests in the displacement seismic amplitude ratio between medium (4.5–8 Hz) and high (8–16 Hz) frequency tremor bands, exhibiting a characteristic rise in the days prior to eruptions. We interpret this as formation of a hydrothermal seal that enables rapid pressurization of shallow groundwater. Applying this model to the 2019 eruption at Whakaari (New Zealand), we describe pressurization of the system in the week before the eruption, and cascading seal failure in the 16 h prior to the explosion. Real-time monitoring for this precursor may improve short-term eruption warning systems at certain volcanoes.

## Techno-Economic feasibility of enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) with partially bridging Multi-Stage fractures for district heating applications

Yu, Pengliang, Dempsey, David, Archer, Rosalind (2022). Techno-Economic feasibility of enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) with partially bridging Multi-Stage fractures for district heating applications. Energy Conversion and Management, 257, 115405. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enconman.2022.115405
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-yu-techno-economic-feasibility-enhanced-geothermal/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-yu-techno-economic-feasibility-enhanced-geothermal/yu2022-techno-economic-feasibility.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2022-yu-techno-economic-feasibility-enhanced-geothermal/fulltext.md
We modelled a geothermal heating scheme that forces water through fractured hot rock between two horizontal wells. In a modelled case study at Qiabuqia, China, a 14-fracture design gave a median profit of USD 110 million over 20 years, with a 95% range of USD 24 to 185 million.

- In our model, the permeability of the rock between fractures and the reservoir temperature were the main controls on profitability, with smaller effects from depth and fracture number.
- With other parameters at benchmark values, projects below 120 °C or below 0.4 mD of rock permeability did not return a profit within 20 years.
- Adding fractures along a fixed well length gave diminishing returns, with almost no extra heat output at 16 to 20 fractures.
- At Qiabuqia, a 14-fracture design gave the highest profit, with a median heat output of 52.4 MW sustained over 20 heating seasons.
- In the most favourable permeability case, the 14-fracture design could heat up to 2.8 km² of floor space and displace more than 1.5 million tonnes of CO2 over 20 years.

## Hydrothermal Cooling as a Requirement for Short Storage of Silicic Magmas

Kelly, Liam J., Gualda, Guilherme A. R., Gravley, Darren M., Dempsey, David E. (2021). Hydrothermal Cooling as a Requirement for Short Storage of Silicic Magmas. Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems, 22(9), e2021GC009794. https://doi.org/10.1029/2021gc009794
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-kelly-hydrothermal-cooling-requirement-short-storage/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-kelly-hydrothermal-cooling-requirement-short-storage/kelly2021-hydrothermal-cooling-requirement.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-kelly-hydrothermal-cooling-requirement-short-storage/fulltext.md
Magma for large eruptions in New Zealand's Taupō Volcanic Zone appears to have crystallised within decades to centuries. In our calculations, conduction through rock took over 1,000 years to remove the heat. Circulating groundwater above the magma, with a heat output of about 1,000 MW, could remove it within decades.

- For a 150 km³ magma body several kilometres deep, conduction through the overlying rock removed the heat needed for crystallisation over more than 1,000 years.
- In a model of groundwater flowing above the magma, half of 10,000 random trials lost that heat within 100 years, and 90% within 280 years.
- Most trials that cooled the magma within 100 years needed a heat output two to three times the 470 MW released at Rotorua today.
- At Rotorua's present heat output, a magma body of Mamaku size is unlikely to be cooling over decades beneath the caldera now.
- If the magma was stored as several smaller bodies, heat output similar to today's could cool it within decades to centuries.

Abstract: Large (&gt;50 km 3 ) magma bodies that contribute to caldera‐forming eruptions in the Taupō Volcanic Zone (TVZ), New Zealand have shown evidence for crystallization and storage on the order of decades to centuries prior to eruption. We compare various conductive and convective heat extraction models to determine which is more likely to enable the heat loss required for short magma storage. We conclude that purely conductive models only account for heat loss on millennial or longer timescales. We also show that convective hydrothermal systems with heat output of 1,000 MW in magnitude are required for decadal heat extraction from a large, contiguous magma body; yet, heat output similar to present‐day conditions would be suitable for cooling magma distributed as a patchwork of smaller magma bodies. This study shows the potential connection with heat flow at the surface and the presence of a magma body, providing future directions for monitoring restless calderas in environments with a wealth of hydrothermal activity like the TVZ.

## A three-dimensional coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical numerical model with partially bridging multi-stage contact fractures in horizontal-well enhanced geothermal system

Yu, Pengliang, Dempsey, David, Archer, Rosalind (2021). A three-dimensional coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical numerical model with partially bridging multi-stage contact fractures in horizontal-well enhanced geothermal system. International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences, 143, 104787. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijrmms.2021.104787
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-yu-three-dimensional-coupled-thermo-hydro/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-yu-three-dimensional-coupled-thermo-hydro/yu2021-three-dimensional-coupled.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-yu-three-dimensional-coupled-thermo-hydro/fulltext.md
We propose a geothermal well design in which fractures grow alternately from the injection and production wells and stop short of the other well. In our model, this forces water through the rock between fractures and keeps produced water hotter, for the same mass produced, than fractures joining both wells.

- In our model, partially bridging fractures delivered hotter water than fully bridging fractures for the same mass produced, but produced less water in total.
- At a point midway between two fractures, modelled failure began after 12.5 years with partially bridging fractures and after 14.5 years with fully bridging fractures.
- In our simulations, leaving fracture opening out of the model overestimated the failed rock volume by 10 to 20%. We expect the error to be smaller in deeper systems with higher stresses.
- Stresses from cooling had the largest effect on modelled stress changes. Stresses from fluid pressure had a minor effect and appeared to delay failure.

## Heat Transfer Through the Wairakei‐Tauhara Geothermal System Quantified by Multi‐Channel Data Modeling

Ardid, Alberto, Archer, Rosalind, Bertrand, Edward, Sepulveda, Fabian, Tarits, Pascal, Dempsey, David (2021). Heat Transfer Through the Wairakei‐Tauhara Geothermal System Quantified by Multi‐Channel Data Modeling. Geophysical Research Letters, 48(8), e2020GL092056. https://doi.org/10.1029/2020gl092056
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-ardid-heat-transfer-wairakei-tauhara-geothermal/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-ardid-heat-transfer-wairakei-tauhara-geothermal/ardid2021-heat-transfer-wairakei.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-ardid-heat-transfer-wairakei-tauhara-geothermal/fulltext.md
We combined electrical surveys, clay tests on drill cuttings, and well temperature logs to map the clay layer above the Wairakei-Tauhara geothermal reservoir. We estimate that 380 ± 21 MW of heat passes up through this layer. We treat this as a lower bound on the field's total heat output.

- We mapped the clay cap at Wairakei-Tauhara from 250 magnetotelluric stations, with its depth constrained by clay tests on cuttings from 50 wells.
- Temperatures at the top and bottom of the clay cap averaged 58°C and 199°C, with 95% ranges of about 20 to 120°C and 130 to 250°C.
- A deep electrical conductor at Aratiatia Flats lies in cold rock. We suggest it formed by low-temperature alteration of ignimbrite.
- Conduction alone accounts for 153 ± 18 MW through the clay cap. Including slow upward water flow raises our estimate to 380 ± 21 MW.
- We treat 380 MW as a lower bound on the field's heat output, because it omits heat that leaves the reservoir sideways beneath the cap.

Abstract: To obtain the fullest picture of geothermal systems, it is necessary to integrate different types of data, for example, surface electromagnetic surveys, lithology, geochemistry, and temperature logs. Here, by joint modeling a multichannel data set we quantify the spatial distribution of heat transfer through the hydrothermally altered, impermeable smectite layer that has developed atop the Wairakei‐Tauhara system, New Zealand. Our approach involves first constraining magnetotelluric inversion models with methylene blue analysis (an indicator of conductive clay) and mapping these onto temperature and lithology data from geothermal wells. Then, one‐dimensional models are fitted to the temperature data to estimate heat flux variations across the field. As a result, we have been able to map the primary seal that insulates the geothermal reservoir and estimate the heat flow of the system. The approach could be applied in geothermal provinces around the world with implications for sustainable resource management and our understanding of these magmatic systems.

## Bayesian magnetotelluric inversion using methylene blue structural priors for imaging shallow conductors in geothermal fields

Ardid, Alberto, Dempsey, David, Bertrand, Edward, Sepulveda, Fabian, Tarits, Pascal, Solon, Flora, Archer, Rosalind (2021). Bayesian magnetotelluric inversion using methylene blue structural priors for imaging shallow conductors in geothermal fields. Geophysics, 86(3), E171-E183. https://doi.org/10.1190/geo2020-0226.1
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-ardid-bayesian-magnetotelluric-inversion-methylene-blue/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-ardid-bayesian-magnetotelluric-inversion-methylene-blue/ardid2021-bayesian-magnetotelluric-inversion.pdf
We developed a way to map the clay layer above a geothermal reservoir from electrical surveys, using clay tests on drill cuttings to reduce the range of possible depths. At Wairākei it returned depth ranges for the layer's boundaries and reduced the uncertainty in the depth of its base.

- Our Bayesian inversion returns a range of plausible depths for the top and bottom of the shallow conductor beneath each MT station, using clay tests from wells as prior information.
- In a synthetic test, a deterministic inversion placed the conductor's base about 65 m too shallow near the centre, and clay priors brought our estimate closer to the true base.
- At Wairākei, clay priors left the data fit almost unchanged, and the most constrained prior we tested cut the average bottom-depth uncertainty from 77 m to 54 m.
- Our 12-station Wairākei inversion took about 0.3 hours on four cores, against about 28 hours on 56 cores for a 3D inversion that can also image deeper structure.

## Two-dimensional numerical modelling of strategies to avoid thermal stress induced flow channeling in fractured geothermal reservoirs

Rongved, Mats, Bauer, Andreas, Dempsey, David, Holt, Rune M. (2021). Two-dimensional numerical modelling of strategies to avoid thermal stress induced flow channeling in fractured geothermal reservoirs. Geothermics, 90, 101978. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geothermics.2020.101978
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-rongved-two-dimensional-numerical-modelling-strategies/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-rongved-two-dimensional-numerical-modelling-strategies/rongved2021-two-dimensional-numerical.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2021-rongved-two-dimensional-numerical-modelling-strategies/fulltext.md
Cooling by injected water can concentrate flow into one fracture. In our two-dimensional model of two parallel fractures, flow stayed even or evened out with wider, more alike fractures or a higher injection rate. A high starting rate, or injecting through each fracture in turn, made even flow more likely.

- In our model, flow between two fractures splits by the ratio of their apertures. A narrower fracture with a larger relative aperture gain can regain flow.
- With an initial fracture permeability of 5 × 10^-10 m², flow stayed close to even. At 10^-11 m², one fracture took most of the flow within about two days.
- At 1.5 × 10^-10 m², a tenfold lower injection rate gave uneven flow. A tenfold higher rate gave uneven flow at first, then even flow.
- In our model, a high injection rate for the first 30 days, or injection through each fracture in turn for 100 days each, gave close to even flow.
- Resolving temperature beside the fracture on a finer grid changed the modelled timing of thermal breakthrough.

## Ground motion simulation of hypothetical earthquakes in the upper North Island of New Zealand

Dempsey, David, Eccles, Jennifer D., Huang, Jonney, Jeong, Seokho, Nicolin, Elia, Stolte, Andrew, Wotherspoon, Liam, Bradley, Brendon A. (2020). Ground motion simulation of hypothetical earthquakes in the upper North Island of New Zealand. New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics, 64(4), 570-588. https://doi.org/10.1080/00288306.2020.1842469
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2020-dempsey-ground-motion-simulation-hypothetical-earthquakes/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2020-dempsey-ground-motion-simulation-hypothetical-earthquakes/dempsey2020-ground-motion-simulation.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2020-dempsey-ground-motion-simulation-hypothetical-earthquakes/fulltext.md
We simulated the largest credible earthquakes on two faults near Auckland, Hamilton and Tauranga. Sediment basins beneath the Hauraki Rift and Hamilton amplified slow shaking two to three times. A Wairoa North Fault earthquake gave 0.45 g, almost half of gravity, at Auckland's Mangatawhiri Dam.

- We used a physics-based simulator to model an Mw 7.3 earthquake on the Kerepehi Fault and an Mw 6.6 earthquake on the Wairoa North Fault.
- The Kerepehi scenario gave a mean shaking intensity of MMI 9.5 (violent) at Ngātea, near the Firth of Thames.
- Hamilton received two to three times the slow shaking (2 s period) of Huntly, at a similar distance from the fault, because Hamilton sits above a sediment basin.
- The Wairoa North Fault scenario gave a peak ground acceleration of 0.45 g at the Mangatawhiri Dam, 0.22 g at Auckland Airport, and 0.15 g in the CBD.
- These are planning scenarios with no probability attached. Whether damage follows depends on local soils and structures.

Abstract: The upper North Island of New Zealand has large concentrations of population and infrastructure that make it vulnerable to earthquakes on the Kerepehi and Wairoa North faults. Using a physics‐based simulator, we modelled 0–50 Hz ground motions for M w 7.3 and M w 6.6 characteristic earthquakes on these structures. We considered the effects of low‐velocity basins beneath the Hauraki Rift and the city of Hamilton that can amplify ground shaking. For a Kerepehi Fault earthquake, long period (&gt;1s) shaking was amplified a by factor of two to three in Hamilton and towns near the Firth of Thames. Severe to violent, long duration shaking would occur close to the source with the potential to trigger liquefaction that damages flood defence networks and farmland in the Hauraki Depression. Auckland, Hamilton and Tauranga could experience moderate to very strong shaking. Impacts in Auckland are larger for a Wairoa North Fault earthquake, which could generate peak ground accelerations of 0.5g at reservoir dams in the Hūnua Ranges, 0.2g at the international airport, and 0.1–0.2g at the CBD and port. Road, rail and transmission networks are vulnerable to disruption where they converge at infrastructure hotspots 10 km from the fault in South Auckland.

## Automatic precursor recognition and real-time forecasting of sudden explosive volcanic eruptions at Whakaari, New Zealand

Dempsey, D. E., Cronin, S. J., Mei, S., Kempa-Liehr, A. W. (2020). Automatic precursor recognition and real-time forecasting of sudden explosive volcanic eruptions at Whakaari, New Zealand. Nature Communications, 11(1), 3562. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-17375-2
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2020-dempsey-automatic-precursor-recognition-real-time/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2020-dempsey-automatic-precursor-recognition-real-time/dempsey2020-automatic-precursor-recognition.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2020-dempsey-automatic-precursor-recognition-real-time/fulltext.md
We trained a machine learning model on nine years of seismic tremor from one station at Whakaari. It recognised four-hour tremor bursts before most eruptions. In tests on eruptions withheld from its training, it warned of four of five eruptive episodes, including 17 hours before the fatal 2019 eruption.

- We trained a forecaster on tremor recorded at a single seismic station from 2011 to 2020, and it updates its forecast every 10 minutes.
- In cross-validation at an alert threshold of 0.8, the model warned in advance of five of seven eruptions, including 17 hours before the fatal December 2019 eruption.
- At that threshold, alerts covered 8.5% of the nine years and 8.6% of alerts contained an eruption.
- A stricter threshold of 0.93 reduced the time under alert to 2.5% and raised the share of alerts containing an eruption to 15%, but missed one more eruption.
- The main precursors were tremor bursts lasting about four hours. We suggest these record magma rising beneath the vent and releasing hot gas into the shallow hydrothermal system.

Abstract: Sudden steam-driven eruptions strike without warning and are a leading cause of fatalities at touristic volcanoes. Recent deaths following the 2019 Whakaari eruption in New Zealand expose a need for accurate, short-term forecasting. However, current volcano alert systems are heuristic and too slowly updated with human input. Here, we show that a structured machine learning approach can detect eruption precursors in real-time seismic data streamed from Whakaari. We identify four-hour energy bursts that occur hours to days before most eruptions and suggest these indicate charging of the vent hydrothermal system by hot magmatic fluids. We developed a model to issue short-term alerts of elevated eruption likelihood and show that, under cross-validation testing, it could provide advanced warning of an unseen eruption in four out of five instances, including at least four hours warning for the 2019 eruption. This makes a strong case to adopt real-time forecasting models at active volcanoes.

---

## Response of Induced Seismicity to Injection Rate Reduction: Models of Delay, Decay, Quiescence, Recovery, and Oklahoma

Dempsey, David, Riffault, Jeremy (2019). Response of Induced Seismicity to Injection Rate Reduction: Models of Delay, Decay, Quiescence, Recovery, and Oklahoma. Water Resources Research, 55(1), 656-681. https://doi.org/10.1029/2018wr023587
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2019-dempsey-response-induced-seismicity-injection-rate/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2019-dempsey-response-induced-seismicity-injection-rate/dempsey2019-response-induced-seismicity.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2019-dempsey-response-induced-seismicity-injection-rate/fulltext.md
We modelled how injection-triggered earthquakes respond to a cut in injection rate. The earthquake rate can fall by more than the cut and stop for a time before it partly recovers. For Western Oklahoma, our forecasts suggest the 2016 volume limit is inadequate.

- When faults need a minimum pressure rise before they slip, cutting injection reduces the earthquake rate by more than the size of the cut.
- After a cut, earthquakes can stop for a period and then partly return, reaching up to 25% of the pre-cut rate in the paper's examples.
- Calibrated to Western Oklahoma, our model reproduced the onset of earthquakes in early 2014, the peak in 2016, and the decline to September 2018.
- In our forecasts at the September 2018 rate, the chance of magnitude 5 or larger before 2025 was 14 to 46%, and 81 to 90% at the mandated maximum.
- Halving injection to 1.5 million cubic metres a month returned the earthquake rate to background levels between mid-2019 and mid-2021 in our forecasts.

Abstract: When injection‐induced seismicity poses a risk to communities, it is common to reduce the injection rate or halt operations. This applies both to individual wells and well clusters, such as those within the Area of Interest for Triggered Seismicity in Western Oklahoma, where in 2016 a 40% volume reduction mandate was imposed by the state regulator. Here we quantify how induced seismicity responds to an injection reduction. We introduce models of pressure diffusion in idealized geometries coupled to steady state pressurization and rate‐state models of earthquake triggering. We find that the delay in seismicity onset and then postreduction behavior—decay, sometimes quiescence, and recovery of the seismicity rate—depend on the critical triggering pressure and on diffusion and rate‐state parameters. We have adapted our model to replicate the timing of onset, peak, and recent pace of decline of seismicity triggered by wastewater injection in Western Oklahoma. Our analysis implies that diffusivity in the Arbuckle formation is high (between 44 and 277 m2/s). The critical triggering pressure is inferred to be between 0.021 and 0.077 MPa, and fluid overpressure at 4.5‐km depth in the basement is estimated to have increased by as much as 0.190 MPa. We simulate future seismicity out to 2025 for three scenarios. Fixing the 2018 injection rate, already less than the limit imposed by the state regulator, we find a high likelihood of further M ≥ 5 earthquakes. This suggests that the volume reduction mandate in Western Oklahoma is, at present levels, inadequate.

## Microseismicity Cloud Can Be Substantially Larger Than the Associated Stimulated Fracture Volume: The Case of the Paralana Enhanced Geothermal System

Riffault, Jeremy, Dempsey, David, Karra, Satish, Archer, Rosalind (2018). Microseismicity Cloud Can Be Substantially Larger Than the Associated Stimulated Fracture Volume: The Case of the Paralana Enhanced Geothermal System. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 123(8), 6845-6870. https://doi.org/10.1029/2017jb015299
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2018-riffault-microseismicity-cloud-can-substantially-larger/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2018-riffault-microseismicity-cloud-can-substantially-larger/riffault2018-microseismicity-cloud-can.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2018-riffault-microseismicity-cloud-can-substantially-larger/fulltext.md
During the 2011 Paralana geothermal stimulation in South Australia, earthquakes occurred up to 400 m from the well. Our inversion of the earthquake and well data suggests that permeability increased only within 40 m of it. For the best-fitting model, the stimulated volume was 0.4% of the seismically active volume.

- At Habanero in 2003, the density of earthquake hypocentres near the well rose linearly with injection pressure. This supports its use as a proxy for fluid pressure.
- At Paralana, two permeability scenarios, extending 50 m and 400 m from the well, both reproduced the measured rise in injectivity. Only the earthquake data separated them.
- Our inversion suggests that permeability at Paralana increased no further than 40 m from the well, while earthquakes were triggered up to 400 m away.
- For the best-fitting model, permeability at the well rose by a factor of about 30. The stimulated volume was 0.4% of the seismically active volume.
- We suggest that slip on existing fractures was not the main cause of the injectivity increase at Paralana. Acid injection, cooling of the rock, or hydraulic fracturing are more likely causes.

Abstract: The goal of hydraulic stimulation is to increase formation permeability in the near vicinity of a well. However, there remain technical challenges around measuring the outcome of this operation. During two enhanced geothermal system stimulations in South Australia, Paralana in 2011 and Habanero in 2003, extensive catalogs of microseismicity were recovered. It is often assumed that shear failure of existing fractures is the main mechanism behind both the induced earthquakes and any permeability enhancement. This underpins a common notion that the seismically active volume is also the stimulated reservoir. Here we compute the density of earthquake hypocenters and provide evidence that, under certain conditions, this spatiotemporal quantity is a reasonable proxy for pore pressure increase. We then apply an inverse modeling approach that uses the earthquake observations and a modified reservoir simulator to estimate the parameters of a permeability evolution relation. The regime implied by the data indicates that most permeability enhancement occurred very near to the wellbore and was not coincident with the bulk of the seismicity, whose volume was about 2 orders of magnitude larger. Thus, we conclude that, in some cases, it is possible for permeability enhancement and induced seismicity to be decoupled, in which case the seismically active volume is a poor indicator of the stimulated reservoir. Our results raise serious questions about the effectiveness of hydroshearing as a stimulation mechanism in enhanced geothermal system. This study extends our understanding of the complex processes linking earthquakes, fluid pressure, and permeability in both natural and engineered settings.

---

## Physics‐based forecasting of induced seismicity at Groningen gas field, the Netherlands

Dempsey, David, Suckale, Jenny (2017). Physics‐based forecasting of induced seismicity at Groningen gas field, the Netherlands. Geophysical Research Letters, 44(15), 7773-7782. https://doi.org/10.1002/2017gl073878
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2017-dempsey-physics-forecasting-induced-seismicity-groningen/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2017-dempsey-physics-forecasting-induced-seismicity-groningen/dempsey2017-physics-forecasting-induced.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2017-dempsey-physics-forecasting-induced-seismicity-groningen/fulltext.md
We developed a physics-based model of the earthquakes caused by gas extraction at Groningen, calibrated it on about 600 recorded events, and forecast earthquakes from 2017 to 2024. Under each of three extraction rates, the largest event had a 5% chance of exceeding magnitude 4.0.

- Our model represents the 325 largest faults in the Groningen reservoir and the stress changes caused by falling gas pressure.
- Calibration on about 600 earthquakes recorded from 1991 to February 2017 suggests that the reservoir was not critically stressed before production began.
- For February 2017 to 2024, the largest earthquake had a 5% chance of exceeding magnitude 4.0 under extraction rates of 21, 27, and 33 billion cubic metres a year.
- Forecast rates at 33 billion cubic metres a year were about 50% higher than at 21, yet the magnitude with a 10% chance of exceedance moved from 3.82 to 3.89.
- These 10% exceedance magnitudes were 0.3 to 0.4 magnitude units lower than those of a statistical forecast for the same period (Zöller and Holschneider, 2016).

Abstract: Earthquakes induced by natural gas extraction from the Groningen reservoir, the Netherlands, put local communities at risk. Responsible operation of a reservoir whose gas reserves are of strategic importance to the country requires understanding of the link between extraction and earthquakes. We synthesize observations and a model for Groningen seismicity to produce forecasts for felt seismicity (M &gt; 2.5) in the period February 2017 to 2024. Our model accounts for poroelastic earthquake triggering and rupture on the 325 largest reservoir faults, using an ensemble approach to model unknown heterogeneity and replicate earthquake statistics. We calculate probability distributions for key model parameters using a Bayesian method that incorporates the earthquake observations with a nonhomogeneous Poisson process. Our analysis indicates that the Groningen reservoir was not critically stressed prior to the start of production. Epistemic uncertainty and aleatoric uncertainty are incorporated into forecasts for three different future extraction scenarios. The largest expected earthquake was similar for all scenarios, with a 5% likelihood of exceeding M 4.0.

## Simulation of the crystal growth of platelet sea ice with diffusive heat and mass transfer

Wongpan, Pat, Langhorne, Patricia J., Dempsey, David E., Hahn-Woernle, Lisa, Sun, Zhifa (2015). Simulation of the crystal growth of platelet sea ice with diffusive heat and mass transfer. Annals of Glaciology, 56(69), 127-136. https://doi.org/10.3189/2015aog69a777
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-wongpan-simulation-crystal-growth-platelet-sea/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-wongpan-simulation-crystal-growth-platelet-sea/wongpan2015-simulation-crystal-growth.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-wongpan-simulation-crystal-growth-platelet-sea/fulltext.md
We simulated, crystal by crystal and in three dimensions, the loose layer of ice platelets that collects under Antarctic sea ice near ice shelves. In our model the layer is about 22% ice by volume, close to the 25 ± 6% estimated from field heat-flux measurements.

- In our model the sub-ice platelet layer has a solid fraction of about 0.22, in good agreement with 0.25 ± 0.06 from heat-flux measurements (Gough and others, 2012a).
- Halving the diameter of the arriving crystals from 10 mm to 5 mm raised the simulated solid fraction from 0.22 to 0.29.
- When all the crystals arrive at once, c-axes turn towards the horizontal with depth. A continuous supply keeps them randomly oriented. Both patterns agree with McMurdo Sound cores.
- The code reproduces an exact solution for a slab of sea ice freezing downwards (the Stefan problem) for each of four salt diffusivities.

Abstract: Antarctic coastal sea ice often grows in water that has been supercooled by interaction with an ice shelf. In these situations, ice crystals can form at depth, rise and deposit under the sea-ice cover to form a porous layer that eventually consolidates near the base of the existing sea ice. The least consolidated portion is called the sub-ice platelet layer. Congelation growth eventually causes the sub-ice platelet layer to become frozen into the sea-ice cover as incorporated platelet ice. In this study, we simulate these processes in three dimensions using Voronoi dynamics to govern crystal growth kinetics. Platelet deposition, in situ growth and incorporation into the sea-ice cover are integrated into the model. Heat and mass transfer are controlled by diffusion. We extract and compare spatial-temporal distributions of porosity, salinity, temperature and crystallographic c-axes with observations from McMurdo Sound, Antarctica. The model captures the crystallographic structure of incorporated platelet ice as well as the topology of the sub-ice platelet layer. The solid fraction, which has previously been poorly constrained, is simulated to be ∼0.22, in good agreement with an earlier estimate of 0.25 ± 0.06. This property of the sub-ice platelet layer is important for biological processes, and for the freeboard-thickness relationship around Antarctica.

## Collective properties of injection‐induced earthquake sequences: 2. Spatiotemporal evolution and magnitude frequency distributions

Dempsey, David, Suckale, Jenny, Huang, Yihe (2016). Collective properties of injection‐induced earthquake sequences: 2. Spatiotemporal evolution and magnitude frequency distributions. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 121(5), 3638-3665. https://doi.org/10.1002/2015jb012551
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2016-dempsey-collective-properties-injection-induced-earthquake-sequences/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2016-dempsey-collective-properties-injection-induced-earthquake-sequences/dempsey2016-collective-properties-injection.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2016-dempsey-collective-properties-injection-induced-earthquake-sequences/fulltext.md
In our model, earthquakes triggered by rising fluid pressure include a higher proportion of small events than tectonic earthquakes. Pressure lowers the static strength of a fault faster than its residual strength. Modelling the 2010–2011 Guy-Greenbrier sequence in Arkansas, we estimated a fault permeability of 5 × 10⁻¹² m².

- Triggering the same modelled earthquakes by fluid pressure in place of tectonic stress raised the Gutenberg-Richter b value from 1.15 to 1.53.
- As fluid pressure rose on modelled faults, the b value fell from 1.8 to 1.2. It was also higher on faults with lower initial shear stress.
- Injection directly into a modelled fault produced fewer large earthquakes than a Gutenberg-Richter model predicts, because rupture was easier inside the pressurised zone than outside it.
- A model of the Guy-Greenbrier sequence matched its onset and southwest migration with an aquifer permeability of 10⁻¹³ m² and a fault permeability of 5 × 10⁻¹² m².
- In that model, the two disposal wells together triggered more earthquakes than the sum of each well operating alone.

Abstract: Probabilistic seismic hazard assessment for induced seismicity depends on reliable estimates of the locations, rate, and magnitude frequency properties of earthquake sequences. The purpose of this paper is to investigate how variations in these properties emerge from interactions between an evolving fluid pressure distribution and the mechanics of rupture on heterogeneous faults. We use an earthquake sequence model, developed in the first part of this two‐part series, that computes pore pressure evolution, hypocenter locations, and rupture lengths for earthquakes triggered on 1‐D faults with spatially correlated shear stress. We first consider characteristic features that emerge from a range of generic injection scenarios and then focus on the 2010–2011 sequence of earthquakes linked to wastewater disposal into two wells near the towns of Guy and Greenbrier, Arkansas. Simulations indicate that one reason for an increase of the Gutenberg‐Richter b value for induced earthquakes is the different rates of reduction of static and residual strength as fluid pressure rises. This promotes fault rupture at lower stress than equivalent tectonic events. Further, b value is shown to decrease with time (the induced seismicity analog of b value reduction toward the end of the seismic cycle) and to be higher on faults with lower initial shear stress. This suggests that faults in the same stress field that have different orientations, and therefore different levels of resolved shear stress, should exhibit seismicity with different b‐values. A deficit of large‐magnitude events is noted when injection occurs directly onto a fault and this is shown to depend on the geometry of the pressure plume. Finally, we develop models of the Guy‐Greenbrier sequence that captures approximately the onset, rise and fall, and southwest migration of seismicity on the Guy‐Greenbrier fault. Constrained by the migration rate, we estimate the permeability of a 10 m thick critically stressed basement fault to be 5 × 10−12 m2. We also consider alternative scenarios in which only one of the two disposal wells operated and suggest that, due to the wells interacting, total seismicity may be greater than that attributable to each well alone.

---

## Collective properties of injection‐induced earthquake sequences: 1. Model description and directivity bias

Dempsey, David, Suckale, Jenny (2016). Collective properties of injection‐induced earthquake sequences: 1. Model description and directivity bias. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 121(5), 3609-3637. https://doi.org/10.1002/2015jb012550
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2016-dempsey-collective-properties-injection-induced-earthquake/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2016-dempsey-collective-properties-injection-induced-earthquake/dempsey2016-collective-properties-injection.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2016-dempsey-collective-properties-injection-induced-earthquake/fulltext.md
We modelled large catalogues of earthquakes triggered by injecting fluid into a fault. In our model, these ruptures tended to propagate back towards the injection well, where high fluid pressure favours continued rupture. In the strongest case, a sample of three modelled ruptures was enough to detect this bias.

- We coupled a fracture mechanics model of one-dimensional fault rupture with heterogeneous fault stress and simulated fluid pressure around an injection well.
- Modelled tectonic earthquakes mostly ruptured in one direction, equally often either way, with a weaker preference than in 42 observed large shallow earthquakes.
- Injection directly into a fault biased modelled ruptures towards the well, where high fluid pressure lowers the residual strength of the fault.
- The bias was strongest for a pressure front advancing through a stimulated fault and for larger earthquakes, and small when the well was off the fault.
- A statistical test detected the strongest bias in samples of three modelled ruptures, and the weaker bias from radial flow in samples of 20 ruptures above magnitude 2.4.

Abstract: Induced seismicity is of increasing concern for oil and gas, geothermal, and carbon sequestration operations, with several M &gt; 5 events triggered in recent years. Modeling plays an important role in understanding the causes of this seismicity and in constraining seismic hazard. Here we study the collective properties of induced earthquake sequences and the physics underpinning them. In this first paper of a two‐part series, we focus on the directivity ratio, which quantifies whether fault rupture is dominated by one (unilateral) or two (bilateral) propagating fronts. In a second paper, we focus on the spatiotemporal and magnitude‐frequency distributions of induced seismicity. We develop a model that couples a fracture mechanics description of 1‐D fault rupture with fractal stress heterogeneity and the evolving pore pressure distribution around an injection well that triggers earthquakes. The extent of fault rupture is calculated from the equations of motion for two tips of an expanding crack centered at the earthquake hypocenter. Under tectonic loading conditions, our model exhibits a preference for unilateral rupture and a normal distribution of hypocenter locations, two features that are consistent with seismological observations. On the other hand, catalogs of induced events when injection occurs directly onto a fault exhibit a bias toward ruptures that propagate toward the injection well. This bias is due to relatively favorable conditions for rupture that exist within the high‐pressure plume. The strength of the directivity bias depends on a number of factors including the style of pressure buildup, the proximity of the fault to failure and event magnitude. For injection off a fault that triggers earthquakes, the modeled directivity bias is small and may be too weak for practical detection. For two hypothetical injection scenarios, we estimate the number of earthquake observations required to detect directivity bias.

---

## Hydraulic fracturing fluid migration in the subsurface: A review and expanded modeling results

Birdsell, Daniel T., Rajaram, Harihar, Dempsey, David, Viswanathan, Hari S. (2015). Hydraulic fracturing fluid migration in the subsurface: A review and expanded modeling results. Water Resources Research, 51(9), 7159-7188. https://doi.org/10.1002/2015wr017810
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-birdsell-hydraulic-fracturing-fluid-migration-subsurface/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-birdsell-hydraulic-fracturing-fluid-migration-subsurface/birdsell2015-hydraulic-fracturing-fluid.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-birdsell-hydraulic-fracturing-fluid-migration-subsurface/fulltext.md
We modelled fracturing fluid injected into shale 1,500 m below a drinking water aquifer. In our model, no fluid reached the aquifer without a permeable pathway such as a fault or leaky well. Where a pathway existed, modelling well production and imbibition reduced the amount reaching the aquifer tenfold.

- Without a permeable pathway, no fracturing fluid reached the aquifer in our model, and fluid rose on the order of 100 m through intact rock in 1,000 years.
- In our base case with a pathway, 1.2% of the injected fluid reached the aquifer after 1,000 years.
- After 20 years of production, the well had removed 68% of the injected fluid and imbibition had held 13% in the shale.
- With both well production and imbibition removed from the model, 12.3% reached the aquifer, about ten times the base case.
- Less than 10 m of intact seal in an otherwise leaky pathway reduced the amount reaching the aquifer to 0.00006%.

Abstract: Understanding the transport of hydraulic fracturing (HF) fluid that is injected into the deep subsurface for shale gas extraction is important to ensure that shallow drinking water aquifers are not contaminated. Topographically driven flow, overpressured shale reservoirs, permeable pathways such as faults or leaky wellbores, the increased formation pressure due to HF fluid injection, and the density contrast of the HF fluid to the surrounding brine can encourage upward HF fluid migration. In contrast, the very low shale permeability and capillary imbibition of water into partially saturated shale may sequester much of the HF fluid, and well production will remove HF fluid from the subsurface. We review the literature on important aspects of HF fluid migration. Single-phase flow and transport simulations are performed to quantify how much HF fluid is removed via the wellbore with flowback and produced water, how much reaches overlying aquifers, and how much is permanently sequestered by capillary imbibition, which is treated as a sink term based on a semianalytical, one-dimensional solution for two-phase flow. These simulations include all of the important aspects of HF fluid migration identified in the literature review and are performed in five stages to faithfully represent the typical operation of a hydraulically fractured well. No fracturing fluid reaches the aquifer without a permeable pathway. In the presence of a permeable pathway, 10 times more fracturing fluid reaches the aquifer if well production and capillary imbibition are not included in the model.

---

## Numerical modeling of injection, stress and permeability enhancement during shear stimulation at the Desert Peak Enhanced Geothermal System

Dempsey, David, Kelkar, Sharad, Davatzes, Nicholas, Hickman, Stephen, Moos, Daniel (2015). Numerical modeling of injection, stress and permeability enhancement during shear stimulation at the Desert Peak Enhanced Geothermal System. International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences, 78, 190-206. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijrmms.2015.06.003
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-dempsey-numerical-modeling-injection-stress-permeability/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-dempsey-numerical-modeling-injection-stress-permeability/dempsey2015-numerical-modeling-injection.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-dempsey-numerical-modeling-injection-stress-permeability/fulltext.md
In 2010, cold water injected below the pressure that opens fractures raised the injectivity of well 27-15 at Desert Peak by an order of magnitude. Our model suggests cooling, and the stresses it caused, kept fractures failing where overpressure was too low. Pressure was still needed to push water in.

- Injectivity was stable at wellhead pressures up to 2.4 MPa and rose only at 3.1 MPa. Our model reproduces the absence of stimulation and approximately captures the timing of the onset.
- At the low pressure steps, water left the well only about 20 °C cooler than the rock. In our model, this was too little cooling to make fractures slip.
- Overpressure fell off quickly with distance from the well. In our model, cooling and the stresses it caused beyond the cold rock kept fractures failing further out.
- From 18 m to the edge of the failure front at 30 m, stress changes outside the cooled rock contributed most to modelled failure. These stresses are probably overestimated, because the model cannot represent tensile failure.
- Late in the 3.1 MPa step, injectivity gains were small, but the modelled stimulated volume kept growing with the volume of cold water injected.

## Reducing uncertainty associated with CO2 injection and brine production in heterogeneous formations

Dempsey, David, O’Malley, Daniel, Pawar, Rajesh (2015). Reducing uncertainty associated with CO2 injection and brine production in heterogeneous formations. International Journal of Greenhouse Gas Control, 37, 24-37. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijggc.2015.03.004
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-dempsey-reducing-uncertainty-associated-co2-injection/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-dempsey-reducing-uncertainty-associated-co2-injection/dempsey2015-reducing-uncertainty-associated.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2015-dempsey-reducing-uncertainty-associated-co2-injection/fulltext.md
When CO2 is injected while brine is pumped out nearby, unknown variations in rock permeability make the outcome hard to predict. In a synthetic reservoir, permeability measured at five wells narrowed 30-year prediction ranges by 40 to 72%. Pressure tests between wells narrowed two of these ranges further.

- In our synthetic reservoir, fast flow paths brought CO2 to two of four production wells within about 11 years, whereas a uniform model predicted no arrival within 30 years.
- Permeability measured at five wells narrowed the 30-year prediction ranges for CO2 retention, brine production and CO2 production by 40, 45 and 72%.
- Weighting model runs by their match to simulated interference tests narrowed the brine and CO2 production ranges by a further 38 and 69%.
- After weighting, the ranges of predicted CO2 arrival time were narrower and included the true time at three of the four production wells.
- At the remaining well, a small permeable zone inside a larger region of low-permeability rock meant its CO2 arrival was still not predicted.

## Passive injection: A strategy for mitigating reservoir pressurization, induced seismicity and brine migration in geologic CO2 storage

Dempsey, David, Kelkar, Sharad, Pawar, Rajesh (2014). Passive injection: A strategy for mitigating reservoir pressurization, induced seismicity and brine migration in geologic CO2 storage. International Journal of Greenhouse Gas Control, 28, 96-113. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijggc.2014.06.002
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-dempsey-passive-injection-strategy-mitigating-reservoir/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-dempsey-passive-injection-strategy-mitigating-reservoir/dempsey2014-passive-injection-strategy.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-dempsey-passive-injection-strategy-mitigating-reservoir/fulltext.md
We propose passive injection, in which pumping brine out of a reservoir draws CO2 in without raising reservoir pressure. In our models, a closed reservoir 3 km deep stored up to about 4 million tonnes of CO2 a year, with about 1.7 tonnes of brine produced per tonne stored.

- In our simulations, reservoir pressure never rose above its starting value, and the stress driving faults towards slip fell everywhere except close to injection wells.
- After allowing for model resolution, storage reached about 4 million tonnes of CO2 a year in a four-stage operation with wells 1 km apart.
- Beyond the first stage, about 1.7 tonnes of brine were produced per tonne of CO2 stored, and roughly twice that in a reservoir open at its edges.
- Time to CO2 breakthrough grew roughly with the square of well spacing and was roughly inversely proportional to the pumping pressure.
- At an estimated US$2.50 to US$25.00 per tonne of CO2 for brine treatment and disposal, the method would need favourable disposal conditions, other revenue or economies of scale.

Abstract: Many technical, regulatory and public perception challenges remain to be addressed before large-scale deployment of CO2 geologic storage becomes a reality. Two major risks associated with injection of CO2 into the subsurface are the possibility of induced earthquakes compromising long-term seal integrity, and the displacement of saline brines resulting in contamination of shallow groundwater. Both induced seismicity and brine migration are caused by elevated pressures in the storage formation owing to the relative incompressibility of water. Here, we describe a strategy, termed passive injection that can be used to inject large amounts of CO2 in a storage formation with no increase, temporary or long-term, in reservoir pressure. Passive injection relies on the strategic placement of brine production wells to create negative pressure gradients that result in CO2 entering the formation at ambient pressure. Injection occurs at the intersection of pressure-depth profiles for a surface-pressurized, low-density CO2 column and a hydrostatic column of formation fluid. A multi-stage, square-ring well configuration is envisaged, in which brine production wells are repurposed for CO2 injection upon CO2 breakthrough, and the next concentric ring of production wells installed at a greater distance. Numerical simulations of passive injection are presented using the coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM), multi-fluid, multi-phase numerical simulator FEHM. We consider CO2 injection into a 3 km-deep, closed reservoir over a period of 50 years, with up to four stages of injection and production depending on well-spacing and production pressures. Storage rates as high as 4 Mt yr−1 at 70% utilization of the reservoir pore volume are achieved under optimum conditions. Long-term mass production of brine is approximately 1.7 times that of CO2 sequestered. Geomechanical effects due to reservoir drawdown, cooling near injection wells, and surface subsidence are modeled. The risk of induced seismicity is quantified in terms of the Coulomb Failure Stress (CFS) for an optimally oriented fault in an extensional tectonic regime. Injection and production-induced changes in pressure and CFS confirm that, both during and at the conclusion of injection, (i) reservoir pressure is everywhere less than or equal to its initial value; and (ii) the risk of induced seismicity is everywhere reduced or unchanged. Thus, the primary risks of brine migration outside the primary reservoir and induced seismicity compromising seal integrity are neutralized. Passive injection produces large quantities of brine, the treatment and disposal of which represents an additional economic burden to CO2 geologic storage operations. Unless additional revenue streams or economies of scale can be leveraged, these costs are likely to limit the viability of the proposed scheme to only the most economically favorable sites.

---

## Insights into interconnections between the shallow and deep systems from a natural CO2 reservoir near Springerville, Arizona

Keating, Elizabeth, Newell, Dennis, Dempsey, David, Pawar, Rajesh (2014). Insights into interconnections between the shallow and deep systems from a natural CO2 reservoir near Springerville, Arizona. International Journal of Greenhouse Gas Control, 25, 162-172. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijggc.2014.03.009
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-keating-insights-interconnections-shallow-deep-systems/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-keating-insights-interconnections-shallow-deep-systems/keating2014-insights-interconnections-shallow.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-keating-insights-interconnections-shallow-deep-systems/fulltext.md
At a natural CO2 reservoir in Arizona, a permeable fault likely connects the deep gas to a shallow aquifer. Water chemistry suggests that CO2 rises dissolved in saline water that also contains arsenic. In our simulations, most of the gas remains at depth despite the fault.

- A groundwater model matched drawdowns from decades of pumping best when the fault zone was distinct, permeable and extended through the full model thickness.
- Chloride, sulfate, bicarbonate, lithium, rubidium and arsenic rise together in the production wells, consistent with saline, CO2-rich water from depth mixing with dilute groundwater.
- Arsenic was the only trace element above the US drinking water limit, reaching 0.042 mg/l, about four times the 0.010 mg/l limit.
- In a simple degassing model, a loss of 40–50% of the dissolved CO2 can account for the carbon isotopes of the most concentrated groundwater.
- Simulated gas rose along the fault within 300 days. Scaled to a 50 km fault, the later leak would empty a dome-sized reservoir in about 2,800 years without resupply.

Abstract: If carbon dioxide (CO2) sequestration into deep geologic reservoirs is to be accepted by the public and environmental regulators, the possibility of upward leakage into shallow groundwater should be acknowledged and those processes well-understood. Studies of natural CO2 reservoirs and their connection (or lack thereof) with the shallow subsurface is one way to explore these issues. A natural reservoir near Springerville, Arizona has leaked CO2 to the surface along a fault zone for thousands of years, creating large travertine deposits. In recent times, the CO2 leak rates have declined significantly yet the shallow aquifer is still highly enriched in CO2. In this study, using water level data and simulations we demonstrate that the fault zone likely provides hydrologic communication between the shallow aquifer and the deeper reservoir. It is reasonable to assume, therefore, that the source of the CO2 in wells completed within the fault zone is the deeper CO2 reservoir. We present water chemistry data to demonstrate the geochemical impact of this CO2 on shallow groundwater quality. Interestingly, arsenic concentrations are elevated, but other trace metals concentrations are not. Arsenic and chloride concentrations co-vary, suggesting perhaps an external source of both elements rather than an in situ release of As due to CO2 attack on shallow aquifer sediments. Observations at this site demonstrate that hydraulic communications between shallow and deep layers and upward CO2 migration does not preclude long-term viability of a substantial CO2 reservoir at depth. We present multi-phase flow simulations to illustrate possible mechanisms trapping the CO2 at depth. Collectively, these analyses show that some degree of upward CO2 leakage may not be necessarily incompatible with the overarching goals of sequestering CO2 and protecting shallow groundwater.

---

## Modeling caprock bending stresses and their potential for induced seismicity during CO2 injection

Dempsey, David, Kelkar, Sharad, Pawar, Rajesh, Keating, Elizabeth, Coblentz, David (2014). Modeling caprock bending stresses and their potential for induced seismicity during CO2 injection. International Journal of Greenhouse Gas Control, 22, 223-236. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijggc.2014.01.005
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-dempsey-modeling-caprock-bending-stresses-their/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-dempsey-modeling-caprock-bending-stresses-their/dempsey2014-modeling-caprock-bending.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2014-dempsey-modeling-caprock-bending-stresses-their/fulltext.md
In our models, CO2 injection at overpressures of 5 to 10 MPa bent the caprock and induced stresses of about 1 to 2 MPa in it, outside the zone of raised fluid pressure. Such stresses would be enough to reactivate an undetected, well-oriented, critically stressed fault near the well.

- In our models, overpressures of 5 to 10 MPa induced caprock stresses of about 1 to 2 MPa, in rock where the fluid pressure change was small.
- Doming of the caprock reduced horizontal compression in the same direction as the regional tectonic extension at the Springerville analogue site.
- Raising the injection overpressure from 5 to 15 MPa increased the peak Coulomb failure stress change in the caprock from 1.2 to 3.5 MPa.
- With several interacting wells, injecting around a known hazardous fault may not avoid loading it.
- We propose that limits on injection pressure also consider how far the overpressured region spreads.

## Hydrological effects of dip‐slip fault rupture on a hydrothermal plume

Dempsey, D. E., Archer, R. A., Ellis, S. M., Rowland, J. V. (2013). Hydrological effects of dip‐slip fault rupture on a hydrothermal plume. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 118(1), 195-211. https://doi.org/10.1029/2012jb009395
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2013-dempsey-hydrological-effects-dip-slip-fault/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2013-dempsey-hydrological-effects-dip-slip-fault/dempsey2013-hydrological-effects-dip.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2013-dempsey-hydrological-effects-dip-slip-fault/fulltext.md
We modelled a hot-water plume beside a normal fault in New Zealand's Taupō Volcanic Zone. A modelled magnitude 5.7 earthquake tripled water outflow, but within 20 days the excess fell below 10% of natural outflow. Fault damage caused a lasting rise in flow and moved upflow away from the fault.

- Before rupture, a fault core 10,000 times less permeable than the rock around it split the plume into two upflows, with 10 MW of heat conducted across the fault between them.
- Horizontal compression of rock near the surface during the modelled earthquake of about magnitude 5.7 increased water outflow from 360 to about 1,100 kg/s.
- This excess outflow halved within 2.6 days and was less than 10% above the natural rate after about 20 days.
- Damage to the fault core raised outflow by 14 to 15 kg/s over the 10 years modelled and let hot water rise across the fault.
- Heat crossing the fault rose from 10 MW to 215 MW at rupture, and upflow moved from the footwall scarp into the hanging wall.

Abstract: Earthquakes cause a variety of hydrological effects, including changes in well levels, streamflow, hot‐spring temperatures, and geyser periodicity. These may be produced by changes in pore‐fluid pressure or by changes in permeability. We investigate near‐field effects of normal earthquakes on fault‐controlled hydrothermal plumes, e.g., at the Te Kopia geothermal system on the Paeroa Fault, New Zealand. A numerical model is detailed that addresses the effects of coseismic pore‐pressure and permeability perturbations on geothermal upflow along a dip‐slip fault. Fluid flow is modeled using the heat and mass transfer code Finite Element Heat and Mass transfer. The 2 m wide fault is impermeable and thus behaves as a partition between fluid flow in the adjacent fault blocks, as well as a structure for upflow to localize upon. A realistic distribution for the coseismic change in mean rock stress is obtained from a plane‐strain mechanical model for normal fault rupture in an elastic‐plastic‐viscous crust. These stress changes are imported into the fluid flow model as pore‐fluid pressure changes. In addition, we consider the effects of fault core fracture and damage by introducing an increase in permeability at the fault plane. Results show that short‐term effects are dominated by pore‐pressure changes, which cause increased heat and mass fluxes at the surface for a period of several weeks. Longer‐term, an elevated mass flux remains due to the increase in subsurface permeability. Upflow migrates from the footwall scarp into the hanging wall and away from the fault, because rising fluids are no longer deflected by the fault.
