## Delineation of catchment zones of geothermal systems in large‐scale rifted settings

Dempsey, D. E., Simmons, S. F., Archer, R. A., Rowland, J. V. (2012). Delineation of catchment zones of geothermal systems in large‐scale rifted settings. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 117(B10), 2012JB009515. https://doi.org/10.1029/2012jb009515
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-delineation-catchment-zones-geothermal-systems/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-delineation-catchment-zones-geothermal-systems/dempsey2012-delineation-catchment-zones.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-delineation-catchment-zones-geothermal-systems/fulltext.md
We modelled circulation in a rift like New Zealand's Taupō Volcanic Zone and traced water from ten modelled geothermal fields to where it entered the ground. Their catchments cover 70 to 500 km² and increase with field heat output. Most water spends 5,000 to 50,000 years underground.

- We traced 1.7 million flow paths backwards through a 3-D model of rift-scale circulation, from ten modelled geothermal fields to where their water entered the ground.
- Most water spent 5,000 to 50,000 years underground, and water younger than 5,000 years entered the ground within 1 to 2 km of a field.
- Catchments of 70 to 500 km² overlapped little, were asymmetric about their fields, and increased in area in proportion to field heat output.
- A Voronoi construction based only on field positions and heat outputs approximately reproduced the main features of the modelled catchments.
- Applied to the TVZ, the method leaves an empty region near the Horohoro prospect, large enough for the catchment of a system of up to 400 MW.

Abstract: Hydrothermal convection in the Taupo Volcanic Zone (TVZ), New Zealand, is driven by heat extracted at the brittle‐ductile transition, which is in turn supplied by magmatic intrusion of the lower‐crust. We present a numerical model that approximates this circulation in a statistical sense, being constrained by TVZ dimensions and mean thermal properties, but incorporating a permeability distribution of arbitrary heterogeneity. A particle tracking methodology that accounts for advective and dispersive transport is introduced, and ensembles of several tens of thousands of flow paths are constructed for each of the modeled geothermal systems. These flow paths reveal the nature of mass recharge in multicell convective systems, and suggest the ages of waters in TVZ geothermal systems vary between 5 and 50 kyr. Flow path ensembles are used to delineate catchments for each of the modeled systems and a method for calculating their areas is introduced. Catchment area is shown to be proportional to system heat output and area, which is consistent with a 1‐D analytical model of heat and mass transfer. As an approximation to catchments delineated by particle tracking, we outline a method of Voronoi tessellation based on the positions and heat outputs of geothermal systems. This method is used to delineate catchments for geothermal systems in the TVZ and Iceland.

## Geometric properties of platelet ice crystals

Dempsey, D.E., Langhorne, P.J. (2012). Geometric properties of platelet ice crystals. Cold Regions Science and Technology, 78, 1-13. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coldregions.2012.03.002
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-geometric-properties-platelet-ice-crystals/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-geometric-properties-platelet-ice-crystals/dempsey2012-geometric-properties-platelet.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-geometric-properties-platelet-ice-crystals/fulltext.md
We cut ten closely spaced slices from Antarctic sea ice and rebuilt its crystals in 3-D. For large, elongated grains, the outline in a photograph gave the horizontal direction of the c-axis with a standard deviation of 6°. Grain shape can also depend on the angle of the cut.

- Ten horizontal thin sections, about 9 mm apart, sampled 108 crystals as 249 grains in 400 cm³ of sea ice from McMurdo Sound, Antarctica.
- An ellipse fitted to each grain outline gave the horizontal direction of the c-axis with a standard deviation of 28.9° for all grains and 6.0° for large, strongly elongated grains.
- Slicing the reconstructed crystals at different angles showed that the difference between two ice fabrics we distinguish may depend largely on the plane of the cut.
- At one serrated boundary, the serrations appeared to follow the planes in which ice grows fastest. We propose they form by repeated growth of new layers in grooves between crystals.

## The role of frictional plasticity in the evolution of normal fault systems

Dempsey, David E., Ellis, Susan M., Rowland, Julie V., Archer, Rosalind A. (2012). The role of frictional plasticity in the evolution of normal fault systems. Journal of Structural Geology, 39, 122-137. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsg.2012.03.001
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-role-frictional-plasticity-evolution-normal/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-role-frictional-plasticity-evolution-normal/dempsey2012-role-frictional-plasticity.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-role-frictional-plasticity-evolution-normal/fulltext.md
We modelled a single normal fault in a stretching crust. In our model the fault takes up about half of the stretching of the upper crust. Slow frictional shearing takes up the rest, mostly in the hanging wall, where we suggest new faults are favoured to form.

- In our model, a fault dipping at 50° takes up about half of the upper-crust extension over a 220-year earthquake cycle. Distributed frictional shearing takes up the rest.
- Repeated earthquakes hold the crust next to the fault up to 10 MPa below failure. This stress shadow extends further into the footwall than into the hanging wall.
- Shear bands dipping at about 45° form in the hanging wall, outside the stress shadow, and dip the same way as the main fault. We suggest they can be regarded as proto-faults if they lengthen each time they slip.
- The modelled fault rotates to a shallower dip at about 23.5° per million years, split almost equally between the periods between earthquakes and the earthquakes themselves.
- Our results are consistent with faulting migrating into the hanging walls of older faults, as described for the western Gulf of Corinth, Greece.

## Modeling the effects of silica deposition and fault rupture on natural geothermal systems

Dempsey, D. E., Rowland, J. V., Zyvoloski, G. A., Archer, R. A. (2012). Modeling the effects of silica deposition and fault rupture on natural geothermal systems. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 117(B5), 2012JB009218. https://doi.org/10.1029/2012jb009218
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-modeling-effects-silica-deposition-fault/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-modeling-effects-silica-deposition-fault/dempsey2012-modeling-effects-silica.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-modeling-effects-silica-deposition-fault/fulltext.md
We modelled a geothermal field in New Zealand's Taupō Volcanic Zone where cooling water deposits silica. Over 120,000 years, a low-permeability layer about 200 m thick formed at the surface. It diverted water sideways and warmed the reservoir. A fault rupturing the layer took at least 10,000 years to reseal.

- We coupled a model of heat and water flow in a geothermal field to silica deposition, so that rock porosity and permeability changed as silica filled the pores.
- After 120,000 years, a cap 1 to 2 km across and up to about 200 m thick had formed at the surface above the rising hot water.
- The cap reduced field heat output from 120 to 80 MW, more than tripled the field's area, and raised the heat stored in the reservoir by about 20%.
- In a second model, fault rupture through the cap raised heat output from 75 to 125 MW, but output returned to 75 MW within 1,000 to 2,000 years.
- Because the Paeroa Fault at Te Kopia ruptures about every 1,000 to 2,000 years, renewed flow along the fault may be the usual state of that field.

Abstract: Natural geothermal convection abounds within the Taupo Volcanic Zone (TVZ) of New Zealand's Central North Island. In many locations the highly porous eruptive products that blanket the landscape have been altered by the throughput of hydrothermal fluids and the consequent deposition of silica. We detail a numerical model that considers the evolution of a geothermal plume in the presence of silica deposition/dissolution that controls an evolving permeability distribution. Precipitation of silica occurs according to a gradient reaction regime, in which the dissolved silica concentration is controlled by the temperature dependent silica solubility. Over a period of 120 kyr, continuous geothermal circulation leads to the development of a low permeability cap‐zone, approximately 200 m thick, above the main geothermal upflow zone. The cap‐zone encourages lateral flow of rising fluids, increasing the area across which geothermal expression is observed. It also has an insulating effect on fluids below the cap, causing increases in temperature, enthalpy, and the reservoir potential of the field. A second model is constructed to consider the specific scenario of fault rupture through the impermeable cap‐zone. Coseismic increases in permeability along the fault plane produce vigorous, renewed flow through the center of the geothermal field, temporarily reducing lateral flows. However, resealing of near surface permeability is rapid, and the restoration of lateral flows and recovery of the geothermal reservoir occurs within ∼10 kyr. These effects are discussed in the context of two TVZ geothermal fields: the extinct Ohakuri field, and Te Kopia, which is situated on a major active normal fault.

## Energetics of normal earthquakes on dip-slip faults

Dempsey, David, Ellis, Susan, Archer, Rosalind, Rowland, Julie (2012). Energetics of normal earthquakes on dip-slip faults. Geology, 40(3), 279-282. https://doi.org/10.1130/g32643.1
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-energetics-normal-earthquakes-dip-slip/ | PDF (Accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed, author's version)): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-energetics-normal-earthquakes-dip-slip/dempsey2012-energetics-normal-earthquakes.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2012-dempsey-energetics-normal-earthquakes-dip-slip/fulltext.md
We modelled a normal fault in a stretching crust and quantified where energy is released and taken up during each earthquake. Stored elastic energy lifts the footwall. The hangingwall drops under gravity and compresses the crust. We suggest the energy for normal faulting comes from gravity and stored elastic energy.

- Between earthquakes, the total elastic strain energy in our model crust decreases, although it increases locally in the footwall at mid-crustal depths.
- During an earthquake, the footwall releases about 0.85 TJ of strain energy. Of this, 0.43 TJ lifts the footwall, 0.14 TJ heats the fault and 0.28 TJ pushes the hangingwall.
- The falling hangingwall releases about 1.0 TJ of gravitational potential energy. This is the main source of work that compresses the crust and adds about 1.3 TJ of strain energy.
- Elastic strain energy increases through much of the upper crust during an earthquake. As the fault blocks move apart, each pushes horizontally against the crust beyond it.
- We suggest tectonic stretching triggers normal earthquakes by shifting the balance of forces on the fault, and the energy they release comes from gravity and stored elastic strain.

Abstract: Research Article| March 01, 2012 Energetics of normal earthquakes on dip-slip faults David Dempsey; David Dempsey 1Department of Engineering Science, University of Auckland, Private Bag 92019, Auckland Mail Centre, Auckland, New Zealand Search for other works by this author on: GSW Google Scholar Susan Ellis; Energetics of normal earthquakes on dip-slip faults. Geology 2012;; 40 (3): 279–282. doi: https://doi.org/10.1130/G32643.1 Download citation file: Ris (Zotero) Refmanager EasyBib Bookends Mendeley Papers EndNote RefWorks BibTex toolbar search Search Dropdown Menu toolbar search search input Search input auto suggest filter your search All ContentBy SocietyGeology Search Advanced Search Abstract That earthquakes release vast quantities of energy is widely accepted; however, the most commonly experienced component, radiated seismic energy, is a minor contribution to the total energy budget. The elastic rebound model for earthquakes recognizes that elastic strain energy does work displacing, deforming, and accelerating the crust, as well as causing frictional heating. In this paper we present an energy budget for dip-slip fault rupture in an extensional tectonic regime. A computational model of an elastic-plastic-viscous crust hosting a single fault, modeled as two surfaces in frictional contact, demonstrates contrasting energy flows between the hanging-wall and footwall fault blocks. Our analysis suggests that in the period leading up to an earthquake, the total strain energy contained within the crust decreases, although a local increase within the footwall at mid-crustal depths is observed. During an earthquake, the footwall is subject to an elastic rebound, whereupon uplift of the fault scarp is caused by a mid-crustal stress drop and elastic expansion that releases strain energy. In contrast, gravitational potential energy released from a subsiding hanging wall does work compressing the wider crust, particularly in the mid-crust at the fault tip. This has the unusual consequence of increasing strain energy throughout much of the upper crust during an earthquake. These counterintuitive energy flows suggest that extensional deformation is caused by stored gravitational potential and elastic strain energy, and not by the external tectonic forcing. ## Evolution of supercooling under coastal Antarctic sea ice during winter

Leonard, Gregory H., Langhorne, Patricia J., Williams, Michael J.M., Vennell, Ross, Purdie, Craig R., Dempsey, David E., Haskell, Timothy G., Frew, Russell D. (2011). ## Observation and modeling of platelet ice fabric in McMurdo Sound, Antarctica

Dempsey, D. E., Langhorne, P. J., Robinson, N. J., Williams, M. J. M., Haskell, T. G., Frew, R. D. (2010). Observation and modeling of platelet ice fabric in McMurdo Sound, Antarctica. Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans, 115(C1), 2008JC005264. https://doi.org/10.1029/2008jc005264
Page: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2010-dempsey-observation-modeling-platelet-ice-fabric/ | PDF (Published version): https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2010-dempsey-observation-modeling-platelet-ice-fabric/dempsey2010-observation-modeling-platelet.pdf | Full text: https://ddempsey.github.io/papers/2010-dempsey-observation-modeling-platelet-ice-fabric/fulltext.md
Ice crystals that grow in supercooled water from beneath Antarctic ice shelves are frozen into sea ice. Using ice cores and a crystal growth model, we infer that western McMurdo Sound received a larger and more persistent supply of these crystals than the east in 2007.

- In late 2007, loose ice platelets were recovered from ocean access holes at the three western sites on our transect, and none appeared at the three eastern sites.
- We identify resumed columnar ice, a coarse crystal type beneath platelet ice, and suggest it forms once platelets stop arriving from the ocean.
- In our model, platelets settling on a flat ice base produced a loose layer with no preferred crystal orientation within about 25 mm of ice growth.
- In our model, a loose platelet layer forms when more than about 5 × 10^5 platelets arrive per square metre per day, with ice growing 10 mm per day.
- Read as a qualitative indication of platelet supply, grain boundary density in the cores implies larger and more persistent platelet fluxes in the west, where the upper ocean was supercooled.

Abstract: During the annual growth of landfast ice in McMurdo Sound, Antarctica, an episodic flux of platelet ice crystals from the ocean contributes to the build up of a porous subice platelet layer, which is steadily incorporated into the sea ice cover as it thickens over winter. In November 2007, we examined the spatial variability of these processes by collecting sea ice cores, with simultaneous oceanographic observations, along an east‐west transect in the sound. Previously identified draped and bladed platelet ice types were observed. In addition, we identify resumed columnar growth which appears to be a result of geometric selection from the subice platelet layer after the arrival of new platelet crystals from the ocean has ceased. A numerical model of mechanical platelet ice processes is developed that predicts crystal texture and c axis distributions, producing virtual incorporated platelet ice with known growth history. This model demonstrates how a disordered subice platelet layer arises from an initially flat interface and suggests that such a layer is more likely to form later in the growth season. The model also suggests how the grain boundary density in incorporated platelet ice responds to changes in the flux of loose platelet crystals from the ocean. Application of this result to our 2007 platelet ice observations indicates that sea ice in western McMurdo Sound is subject to larger and more persistent platelet fluxes than the ice in the east. This is consistent with the pattern of in situ supercooling just beneath the ocean surface.
